# Day 22, Strategy: Sun Tzu, know the enemy and know yourself (The Art of War, roughly 5th century BC)

Picture a pitch meeting. Your team has spent six weeks on a partner proposal. The deck is tight, the numbers are solid, and everyone walks in confident. Twenty minutes later the room is cold. The partner's real priority this year is not growth at all. It is a regulatory cleanup you never asked about. You knew yourself well. You did not know them.

That is the situation Sun Tzu is pointing at with the most quoted line in The Art of War. It comes at the end of chapter 3, and the idea is simple. If you know the enemy and know yourself, you can fight a hundred battles without danger. If you know yourself but not the enemy, you will win some and lose some. If you know neither, you are in trouble every time.

Notice what the claim is not. It is not that knowledge guarantees victory. Sun Tzu says you will not be in peril, which is a weaker and more honest promise. Knowing both sides lets you avoid the fights you would lose and pick the ones you can win. The knowledge buys you good judgment about whether to engage at all, which ties directly back to his earlier point that the best win is the one you never have to fight for.

The two halves are not symmetric, and that is the useful part. Most people assume the hard half is learning about the opponent. Sun Tzu is quietly saying the hard half is often you. Armies overestimate their own readiness. Companies overestimate their own capabilities. A program manager will tell a steering committee the integration is on track because that is what everyone in the room believes. Self knowledge here means an unflattering inventory: what can we actually do, how fast, with what we actually have, and where are we fooling ourselves.

Here is a concrete version. In 1941 Japan knew the US Pacific Fleet very well. Its planners had the ship positions, the Sunday morning patterns, the gaps in the air patrols. What they got wrong was themselves. They assumed Japan could absorb a long industrial war against an opponent with ten times its steel output. The attack was a tactical success and a strategic disaster. Full knowledge of the enemy, partial knowledge of the self.

The strongest objection is that the line is close to empty. Of course knowing more helps. Tell me something I can act on. The second objection is harder: in real conflicts you cannot know the enemy. Clausewitz, whom this track reaches later, built an entire theory around the fog of war, the idea that information in conflict is always late, partial and wrong. Sun Tzu's defenders answer that he never promised full knowledge. He promised that the effort to reduce ignorance on both sides pays off more than almost anything else you can spend on, which is why his book ends with a whole chapter on spies. The critics are right that the line is a principle, not a procedure. It tells you where to look, not what you will find.

In this track we have covered deception, which is about distorting what the enemy knows about you, and winning without fighting, which depends on seeing the whole board. This reading is the foundation under both. You cannot deceive well without knowing how the other side thinks, and you cannot choose not to fight unless you can judge the odds. There is also a link forward to the Game Theory track: a Nash equilibrium is really just what happens when each player knows the other's options and picks accordingly.

Question for the day: pick one counterpart you deal with this week, a vendor, a partner, a colleague in another team. Can you state in one sentence what they actually want right now? If not, which half of Sun Tzu's test are you failing?

Primary source: The Art of War, chapter 3, "Attack by Stratagem," final paragraph. The Lionel Giles translation is free online.
